notice.text: This call is recorded and transcribed. You can ask the business for a copy of your recording.

items: a gas furnace about fifteen years old
a heat pump put in a few years ago
an older water heater in the basement
a crawl space under the kitchen
an older electrical panel in the garage
a big backyard with a fence
central air that is ten years old

writer_rules: Name no equipment brand and no other company: say 'the furnace', 'the water heater', 'the panel'. Prices are rough ranges, never exact quotes. Nothing dangerous is described in detail; for a gas smell the staff member tells the caller to leave the house and call the gas utility's emergency line or 911, and the call moves on.

scenarios.label: Service request
scenarios.brief: The caller has a problem at home that fits the business (a slow drain, no heat, a dead outlet, ants in the kitchen) and wants someone out. The dispatcher asks a few questions, gives the trip fee in rough terms, and books an arrival window on a later day.

scenarios.label: Estimate request
scenarios.brief: The caller wants an estimate for a bigger job (a new water heater, a heat pump, a panel upgrade, a termite treatment). The coordinator asks about the home and books a free estimate visit on a later day.

scenarios.label: Reschedule a visit
scenarios.brief: The caller needs to move an upcoming service visit. The dispatcher finds it and offers another arrival window on a later day.

scenarios.label: Problem came back
scenarios.brief: The problem the business fixed last week has come back. The caller is annoyed but polite. The dispatcher apologizes, checks the job, and books a return visit at no charge under the work guarantee.

scenarios.label: Billing question
scenarios.brief: The caller has a question about an invoice: a line they don't understand, or a payment that hasn't shown up. The coordinator explains and fixes it or promises a corrected invoice.

scenarios.label: Recording request: copy
scenarios.brief: After the recording notice, the caller asks why calls are recorded, who can hear them, and how to get a copy of their recording. The coordinator explains plainly and passes the request to the office manager.

scenarios.label: Recording request: deletion
scenarios.brief: The caller is uncomfortable that the call is recorded and asks for the recording to be deleted. The dispatcher notes the request for the office manager, promises nothing they cannot do, and asks whether the caller still needs service.

scenarios.label: Hang-up on hold
scenarios.brief: The caller starts describing a problem, the dispatcher asks them to hold, and the caller hangs up after waiting, saying they'll find someone else.

scenarios.label: Screened robocall
scenarios.brief: An automated prerecorded pitch calls the dispatch line, offering generic business lead generation that names no company. The dispatcher answers; the call is cut off by the line's screening announcement.

scenarios.label: Wrong number
scenarios.brief: The caller meant to reach someone else (the person named under People, or a kind of business, never a named one). The coordinator says it's the wrong number, and the call ends quickly.

scenarios.label: After-hours emergency
scenarios.brief: The call comes in after the business has closed and is answered by its answering service: a pipe has burst, the heat is out on a cold night, or a breaker keeps tripping. The attendant takes the address only as 'the address on file', a callback number and the problem, and says the on-call technician will call back within the hour.

scenarios.label: Voicemail
scenarios.brief: No one picks up. The first business turn is the office's recorded voicemail greeting. The caller leaves a message with their name, the problem or question and a callback number.
